This study introduces a new class of models termed Temporal-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive models with exogenous covariates (TV-PARX). These models extend the standard Poisson AutoRegressive with exogenous covariates (PARX) framework by allowing both autoregressive coefficients and covariate effects to evolve over time. We outline the model's formulation, propose estimation techniques, and develop methods for forecasting and inference regarding time-varying parameters. The utility of the TV-PARX model is demonstrated through an analysis of daily call volumes at a UK emergency center, followed by a comparison with a competing temporal model. Additionally, we apply the model to a dataset of daily COVID-19 cases in the United States to forecast future trends and assess the statistical significance of shifts in the effects of covariates and seasonal patterns. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/TV-PARX.

Aerosol optical depth (AOD) represents a fundamental atmospheric parameter with significant implications for climate science, air quality management, and the calibration of remote sensing instruments. While ground-based measurements remain the primary method for monitoring AOD, there is growing interest in leveraging stellar photometry to derive high-quality, global, and temporally dense AOD estimates. This paper reviews recent efforts to estimate AOD from stellar photometric data, evaluates the strengths and limitations of these approaches, and outlines potential future directions. We conclude that photometric data can serve as an effective source for generating global, temporally dense AOD estimates, which are valuable for enhancing the calibration of remote sensing instruments and improving atmospheric correction in optical imaging. Furthermore, such data could potentially replace or supplement ground-based observations for creating global AOD products. Nevertheless, achieving the highest precision requires substantial investments in data quality control, calibration, and the development of robust inversion algorithms. Ultimately, the utility of photometric-derived AOD products will depend on their accuracy and precision relative to both ground-based observations and satellite retrievals. To maximize the benefits of these products, it is essential to clearly define their intended applications and associated uncertainties. This review focuses on recent advancements in using stellar photometry for AOD estimation; earlier efforts and their associated literature are documented in Section 3.1.1. The introduction of photometric data for AOD inversion is a promising area that warrants further investigation. We anticipate that future developments in this field will yield significant advantages for atmospheric science, air quality monitoring, and the calibration of imaging systems. For a detailed overview of the literature, readers are directed to the extensive bibliographies in Sections 3.1.1 and 3.2.1. Sampling from the configurational space of large molecules remains a significant challenge, particularly for systems with extensive conformational freedom like proteins. While the Langevin dynamics method has been extensively studied for small systems, its application to large molecules is hindered by the difficulty of maintaining stability over long simulation times. This paper introduces a novel approach to Langevin dynamics that ensures stability without compromising sampling efficiency. We demonstrate that this method enables the sampling of large molecular systems, such as proteins, that were previously inaccessible. Furthermore, we show that this approach accelerates conformational transitions, allowing for the exploration of a broader range of conformational states. Numerical experiments confirm that this new method is both stable and highly efficient, capable of sampling conformational states that were difficult to reach using conventional Langevin dynamics. These findings suggest that this approach could become a valuable tool for investigating conformational changes in large molecules. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi0909/RobustLangevin.

This study introduces a new dataset comprising 100,000 image descriptions authored by individuals, collected from online forums. We evaluate captioning models against these human-written references and find that these descriptions are more lenient than those sourced from Flickr. Furthermore, we observe that the specific origin of the image influences how humans write corresponding descriptions. Finally, we demonstrate that existing evaluation metrics do not always align with human judgments regarding the quality of image descriptions. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/rohitgupta99/CAMION.

This study presents a prediction for the baryon-to-meson ratio in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, based on the statistical hadronization model. The results indicate that, when considering central proton-proton collisions, the chemical freeze-out temperature remains consistent with findings from heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, the baryon-to-meson yields at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV align closely with predictions from the thermal model at $\sqrt{s}=200$ GeV, suggesting that the particle yield ratios in proton-proton collisions are largely independent of the center-of-mass energy. These observations support the hypothesis that baryon-to-meson ratios are governed by the baryon chemical potential ($\mu_{B}$) rather than the collision energy. Consequently, the statistical hadronization model can effectively forecast baryon and meson yields for both proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions. Such predictions are valuable for guiding future experimental searches for exotic hadrons and for enabling the study of baryon and meson spectra in proton-proton collisions. The data files corresponding to the baryon and meson yield measurements from UA5 and ALICE, used in this analysis, are accessible at https://root.cern/doc/master/TFile_Root_72_900.html. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates diverse data sources, ranging from high-precision low-energy measurements to high-energy data with significant theoretical uncertainties. This framework must also accommodate various parametrisation and regularisation schemes. We present a Python-based framework designed to unify these elements, enabling the exploration of numerous fitting strategies. The framework incorporates a wide array of data sources, including recent PDF sets, global fits, and specific data sets. It supports multiple parametrisation forms and orders, as well as various regularisation schemes such as $\overline{\text{MS}}$, AC, and CMW. Furthermore, it accounts for scale-dependent theoretical uncertainties via Hessian and Monte Carlo methods, as well as non-perturbative uncertainties. We demonstrate the framework's capabilities by fitting a simple PDF using distinct strategies and regularisation schemes, and by analysing the impact of theoretical uncertainties from different data sets on the resulting PDF. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AMehta27/PDF_Fitting_Framework.

This study employs the active flame method to simulate a turbulent jet fire subjected to acoustic forcing within a linearized framework. The simulation utilizes a linearized RANS model for the premixing zone and a linearized flame model for the combustion zone. The flame model is derived from a linearized global reaction zone model, which is calibrated using a linearized heat release rate profile. This profile is determined by fitting the global reaction zone model to heat release rate data obtained from Large Eddy Simulations (LES). The resulting linearized model is validated against LES data for a 10 cm diameter, 10 m/s air jet fire with a 15 Hz acoustic forcing amplitude. The findings indicate that the linearized model accurately reproduces the LES-predicted heat release rate oscillations. Furthermore, it correctly captures the amplification of velocity and temperature fluctuations at the flame base and the emergence of a large-scale vortex structure within the flame. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach can effectively simulate the response of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic forcing, provided the forcing amplitude remains small. Consequently, this method offers a computationally efficient alternative to LES for investigating the interaction between acoustic waves and turbulent jet fires. Such simulations could support the development of control strategies aimed at mitigating fire-induced vibrations in industrial gas flames. Additionally, this linearized framework could serve as a foundation for exploring flame response to other types of disturbances, such as wind gusts. To broaden the applicability of this linearized model beyond a specific jet configuration, a data-driven technique for estimating the linearized heat release rate model coefficients is proposed. This would enable the simulation of jet fires with varying configurations, including different diameters and inlet velocities. Ultimately, this research contributes to the advancement of models capable of predicting how turbulent flames react to diverse disturbances, a capability that could prove valuable for safety analyses in industrial settings. The simulations were executed on the HPC system TITAN at NERSC, utilizing the OpenFOAM software. The linearized RANS equations were solved via a finite volume method, while the linearized heat release rate model was incorporated using a data-driven approach. For the LES validation, a pre-existing LES simulation of the same configuration was employed. The linearized heat release rate model coefficients were calculated using MATLAB. The RANS simulation was performed with OpenFOAM, and the simulations were managed using the SimScale platform. Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a nonlocal extension of Einstein-Arnold-Riehl (EAR) gravity, formulated as a geometric field theory where the constitutive connection depends on the nonlocal history of the essential tetrad. We examine the relationship between the essential tetrad and constitutive connection in both EAR and NLG, and analyze the equivalence between NLG and a nonlocal affine theory. The study of rare, low-multiplicity final states at hadron colliders serves as a powerful probe for new physics, offering high sensitivity to heavy new particles through deviations in angular distributions. This paper provides an overview of the search for minor systems—specifically central diffractive events, single and double pomeron exchange, and central exclusive production—at the LHC. It details the associated experimental challenges and outlines the current status of these investigations at ATLAS and CMS. Furthermore, it examines the potential for other LHC experiments to explore these processes and highlights the future prospects for central diffractive and exclusive physics at high-luminosity colliders.

We demonstrate that the recurrence intervals of transient X-ray outbursts in nine Galactic Centre quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries are not random, but rather align with the recurrence periods of their past outbursts documented in literature. Furthermore, we establish that the intervals between past and future outbursts in these nine systems are uniform, indicating that their X-ray variability arises from starved accretion disk instabilities. Conversely, the recurrence periods of nine neutron star X-ray binary transients are irregular, suggesting that their outbursts are driven by different mechanisms. We also show that the intervals between past and future outbursts in nine such systems are irregular, implying that their variability is caused by other mechanisms. These findings suggest that the recurrence periods of outbursts in neutron star X-ray binary transients are irregular, whereas those in Galactic Centre quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries are uniform. Consequently, the variability in Galactic Centre quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries is likely due to starved accretion disk instabilities, while the irregular outbursts in neutron star X-ray binary transients stem from alternative mechanisms. This distinction implies that the term "transient" is inappropriate for Galactic Centre quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries, as their past and future outbursts share the same nature. We propose renaming these systems to "accreting" and "non-accreting" low-mass X-ray binaries at the Galactic Centre to better reflect their current and historical states. Additionally, we suggest that the irregular recurrence intervals of outbursts in nine neutron star X-ray binary transients indicate that their future outbursts will not follow a uniform pattern, making it unlikely that their variability is caused by starved accretion disk instabilities. Instead, their irregular outbursts are likely driven by other mechanisms, and we propose that their variability is best described as "irregular outbursts" rather than "transients." Finally, we argue that the variability in nine low-mass X-ray binary systems at the Galactic Centre, which has been termed "transients," is actually characterized by regular recurrence intervals, and we suggest using the term "recurrent outbursts" to more accurately describe their nature.

Bipartite graphs represent a fundamental concept in graph theory with extensive applications across computer science, mathematics, and engineering. This study introduces a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm designed to partition the vertices of a bipartite graph into two sets, $A$ and $B$, such that the subgraph induced by $A$ contains at most $k$ edges and the subgraph induced by $B$ contains no edges. The algorithm relies on a structural characterization of bipartite graphs that satisfy this specific edge partitioning property. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this characterization can be verified in linear time. Our approach involves identifying a maximal independent set of edges and subsequently applying a dynamic programming method over a tree decomposition of the graph. Finally, we establish that for any graph $G$, the parameter $k$ is bounded by the product of the graph's order and its fractional chromatic number. Consequently, if the order of $G$ is fixed, the problem admits a constant-time solution.

This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a system designed to extend the runtime of computationally intensive tasks by dynamically reducing CPU frequency. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on aggressive voltage scaling, HyperDegrade maintains the CPU at its maximum frequency while managing runtime through cycles of rapid frequency drops and quick recoveries. These cycles are optimized based on the specific workload and hardware constraints. Evaluation using a diverse set of workloads demonstrates that HyperDegrade can prolong runtime by up to 2.1×, achieving energy savings comparable to traditional methods. Crucially, it delivers these benefits without increasing runtime, even for workloads that are already optimized for low frequencies. Additionally, the approach offers significant runtime extensions for workloads that cannot be effectively slowed via voltage scaling. Beyond prolonging runtime, HyperDegrade enables other energy-saving strategies, such as shutting down idle cores, to further reduce power consumption. The system is implemented entirely in userspace, requiring no kernel modifications or hardware changes. Source code is available at https://github.com/Pranav-1999/HyperDegrade.

This paper introduces a new unknotting procedure applicable to both classical and welded links, which involves pulling strands through crossings in a specific manner. We demonstrate that this procedure reduces the welded Alexander polynomial for welded links and, for classical links, also lowers their standard crossing number. Consequently, this technique offers an effective method for simplifying unknots within the welded category and can be utilized to construct minimal unknotting sequences for welded links. Additionally, we provide a characterization of unknots in the welded category and present a procedure to transform any unknot into the trivial unknot within the classical category. As an application, we prove that the cinquefoil and stevedore knots are not unknot equivalent in the welded category, whereas the granny and trefoil knots are. Finally, we establish that no unknotting sequence exists for the square knot in the welded category, indicating that the square knot is not trivial in this context. The proposed procedure may also find utility in analyzing entangled structures in biological and chemical systems. Our characterization of unknots in the welded category could serve as a valuable tool for future research in this area.

This paper introduces a tactical multi-agent framework designed to maximize the utility of a team of standard networked robots with limited computational and communication resources, operating within a stochastic dynamic game. The game models a scenario where a team of friendly robots attempts to intercept a target controlled by an adversarial agent, who aims to evade interception. The utility function reflects the trade-off between the time required for interception and the energy consumed by the robots. To address this game, we propose a tabular collaborative learning algorithm that enables the team of standard networked robots to learn an optimal collaborative strategy. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this algorithm converges to an $\epsilon$-Nash Equilibrium (NE) in finite time. Simulation results are presented to validate the proposed framework and algorithm. These results also compare a learning-based collaborative strategy against a greedy strategy, illustrating the advantages of collaboration. Furthermore, the simulations examine how the size of the tabular representation impacts the learning performance of the collaborative strategy. The proposed framework and algorithm are applicable to various tactical scenarios involving teams of standard robots with constrained resources, such as search and rescue missions, border surveillance, and intercepting adversarial agents.

This paper introduces a constructive approach for embedding the direct product $G_1\times G_2$ into the wreath product $H_1\wr G_2$, where $G_1$, $G_2$, and $H_1$ are finite groups. The method relies on decomposing the set $G_1$ into a Cartesian product $A_1\times A_2$ and constructing a regular representation $\rho_1$ of $G_1$ on $A_1\times A_2$ that preserves this product structure. By combining $\rho_1$ with a regular representation of $G_2$ on $G_2$, we induce a representation of $G_1\times G_2$ acting on $A_1\times A_2\times G_2$. Finally, we embed this induced representation into the regular representation of $H_1\wr G_2$ on $A_1\times G_2$. We demonstrate that this construction is optimal when $G_1$ and $G_2$ are abelian $p$-groups and $H_1=G_1$. Additionally, we apply this technique to derive new embedding results for symmetric groups, alternating groups, and finite simple groups of Lie type.

The sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors, such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA, is constrained by seismic noise at low frequencies and thermal noise in optical components at high frequencies. To surpass these limitations and enable the detection of gravitational waves from high-frequency sources, a new topology for interferometric gravitational wave sensors is required. This paper introduces the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a topology that offers superior high-frequency response compared to conventional interferometric sensors. We demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac configuration can achieve a flat frequency response extending up to 100 kHz, utilizing optical components identical to those found in current gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, we show that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer can be implemented with existing interferometric sensors, including the seismic-isolated arms of current detectors. As a proof of concept, we propose integrating a sloshing-Sagnac loop into one arm of a standard interferometric sensor to create a hybrid sensor with enhanced high-frequency response. Finally, we outline the necessary modifications to data analysis pipelines and detector characterization methods required to utilize the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer and its hybrid configurations.

This study introduces a novel non-overlapping visibility area (NOVA) metric to evaluate the visibility region for selecting the optimal access point in XL-MIMO networks. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on non-intersecting visibility graphs, our NOVA metric directly calculates the non-overlapping visibility area. We propose a stochastic access protocol for XL-MIMO networks that utilizes this metric to determine the best access point based on the non-overlapping visibility area. Simulation results demonstrate that the NOVA metric offers a more accurate assessment of non-overlapping visibility regions compared to existing methods. Furthermore, simulations indicate that the NOVA-based stochastic access protocol outperforms both the closest AP-based and random access protocols in terms of throughput. These findings confirm that the NOVA metric provides a superior measure for non-overlapping visibility areas, and the NOVA-based protocol yields significant throughput gains. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/XL-MIMO_Non_Overlapping_Visibility_Area.

Although neural language models have largely superseded $N$-gram models in recent years, they still face challenges in accurately predicting specific words, particularly low-frequency terms. To address this, we introduce a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both neural and $N$-gram models for text generation. Our method employs a BERT-based model to predict residuals, which are then corrected by an $N$-gram model to produce the final output. Extensive experiments on English and Chinese datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our model achieves remarkable results on the TREC factual consistency challenge, surpassing previous best scores by a wide margin. These findings indicate that the $N$-gram model can effectively compensate for the limitations of neural models in predicting specific words. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/lingdust/NGram-Residual-LM.

This work introduces Informed OCR (iOCR), a novel end-to-end trainable framework designed to extract vote totals from scanned images of paper ballots. Unlike conventional OCR methods that rely on character-level predictions, iOCR leverages the inherent structure of vote totals to correct recognition errors. The model employs a hybrid architecture combining a character-level encoder with a symbol-level encoder, trained to predict the final vote count directly from ballot images. Experimental results demonstrate that iOCR surpasses standard OCR solutions, achieving an F1 score of 0.9999 on a public dataset and outperforming both traditional OCR and other deep learning-based approaches on a private dataset. The source code and a user-friendly demo are accessible at https://github.com/PranavBhargavi/iOCR.

This study examines global atmospheric circulation patterns in simplified global circulation models (GCMs) using a comparative approach. We analyze the relationship between planetary rotation rate and frictional forcing, measured by the Rossby number, to identify distinct circulation regimes. Our findings indicate that the atmosphere in these models transitions from cyclostrophic super-rotation at low Rossby numbers to geostrophic turbulence at high Rossby numbers. This shift is driven by the dominance of different forces: cyclostrophic balance gives way to geostrophic balance, and eddy viscosity replaces friction as the primary dissipative mechanism. The transition between these regimes is marked by the emergence of a jet stream, which acts as a boundary separating the super-rotating equatorial region from the turbulent mid-latitudes. In the geostrophic turbulent regime, the atmosphere exhibits a distinct energy cascade characterized by a $k^{-3}$ spectrum, where energy moves from large to small scales. Conversely, the cyclostrophic super-rotating regime displays a $k^{-5}$ spectrum, indicative of an inverse cascade where energy flows from small to large scales. These results align with observations of terrestrial planets and gas giants, as well as exoplanets. Furthermore, the identified circulation regimes offer valuable insights for designing future atmospheric GCMs aimed at extrasolar planets. These regimes can serve as a guide for selecting appropriate physical parameters, such as eddy viscosity and drag coefficients, to accurately simulate the atmospheres of extrasolar planets. To facilitate this, we have developed a simple model that predicts the eddy viscosity coefficient and drag coefficients based on planetary rotation rate, frictional forcing, and atmospheric depth. This model is detailed in the companion paper (Arney et al., 2016), which also provides a comprehensive review of the literature and presents the results of this research. Ultimately, these findings suggest that eddy viscosity and drag coefficients should not be treated as fixed parameters in atmospheric GCMs for extrasolar planets. Instead, they should be dynamically determined by the planetary rotation rate and frictional forcing, potentially varying with latitude and atmospheric depth. Such dynamic determination is essential for realistically simulating the atmospheres of extrasolar planets in GCMs.

This paper presents a novel integral representation for the reciprocal Gamma function, $\Gamma(z)^{-1}$, derived through the regularization of a classical formula originally proposed by Ramanujan. We demonstrate that this new expression is amenable to numerical evaluation and can be employed to compute $\Gamma(z)^{-1}$ across the entire complex plane. Furthermore, we establish a regularized integral form for the product $\Gamma(a)^{-1}\Gamma(b)^{-1}$, which facilitates the derivation of a regularized integral for the Riemann zeta function. Finally, we explore the application of this last result in calculating high-order derivatives of $\zeta(s)$ at negative integers.

Hydrodynamic theories offer a practical framework for simulating complex quantum many-body systems, particularly those involving ultracold atomic gases. This study introduces a novel hydrodynamic approach termed Phase-space Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (QRHD). By combining QRHD with stochastic mean-field quantum Monte Carlo methods, we create a powerful computational tool capable of modeling interacting quantum gases across a wide range of scales. We specifically apply this combined method to a two-dimensional Bose gas, demonstrating that QRHD effectively captures the system's dynamical evolution during a sudden quench of interactions. Furthermore, the QRHD framework provides valuable insights into the dynamics of quantum systems and facilitates the development of more advanced quantum simulation techniques. The implementation of QRHD is detailed within the open-source code QMCBox.

This paper surveys the field of knowledge acquisition through educator-pupil interactions, where an educator answers questions posed by a pupil to construct a structured knowledge base. Such systems are vital for enabling question answering, natural language understanding, and semantic parsing. We begin by defining the educator-pupil framework and detailing the knowledge base construction process. Subsequently, we categorize and examine systems based on the pupil's question formulation methods and the corresponding educator response strategies. Finally, we discuss open challenges and potential future directions within this domain. Our survey offers a comprehensive overview of systems, tasks, and datasets related to knowledge acquisition via educator-pupil interactions, serving as an essential resource for researchers in natural language processing and artificial intelligence. The source code for this survey is accessible at https://github.com/Anushka-1997/Educator-Pupil-Framework-for-Knowledge-Acquisition-. The recommended citation for this work is: Anushka Sharma, Amitabh Das, and Pushpak Bhattacharyya. This work introduces a novel function representation designed to accelerate the computation of the exact minimum potential energy (or most probable explanation) and its constrained optimization within graphical models. By enabling a more efficient recursive calculation of potential functions over subsets of variables, our approach yields significant performance gains. Specifically, we achieve a speedup of approximately a factor of $n/2$ for both the exact minimum potential energy and its constrained optimization, where $n$ represents the total number of variables. To validate these improvements, we conducted extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world graphical models, demonstrating that our representation consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across various tasks, including the exact computation of the minimum potential energy, its constrained optimization, and a range of approximate inference algorithms. Our implementation is made accessible via the open-source library: https://github.com/AmirHosseinKarami/GraphicalModelsOptimization.

This study introduces a novel, exact method for evaluating structured test statistics within the context of structured hypotheses, specifically targeting the family-wise error rate (FWER). The proposed approach utilizes a precise paired-permutation framework to ensure an exact control of FWER. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through simulations and by applying it to real-world data. Furthermore, we offer practical guidance on implementing this exact procedure as a viable alternative to step-down procedures. The code is accessible at https://github.com/chenyuan99/PPE.

The azimuthal anisotropy of hadrons produced in heavy-ion collisions serves as a primary indicator of initial geometric anisotropy, reflecting the collective behavior of the resulting medium. While the elliptic flow coefficient ($e_2$) dominates in non-central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, the triangular flow coefficient ($e_3$) becomes significant in more central events. This study examines the dependence of $e_2$ and $e_3$ on centrality and transverse mass ($m_T$) across a broad range of non-central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport model (AMPT). The results indicate that $e_3$ in Au+Au collisions aligns well with hydrodynamic model predictions, whereas $e_2$ in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions exceeds hydrodynamic expectations. Furthermore, the $e_3$ coefficient in Au+Au collisions is found to be more sensitive to parton energy loss than to hadron energy loss. In contrast, $e_2$ in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions is more strongly influenced by hadron energy loss. These findings suggest that initial-state anisotropies in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions are driven by distinct mechanisms, and that both parton energy loss and hadron energy loss play crucial roles in shaping anisotropic flow in Au+Au collisions. Ultimately, the multiphase nature of the medium appears to be a key factor in generating anisotropic flow in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu systems. (C) 2012 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

This study introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that incorporates a novel point process prior for target birth, termed the partially grid-oriented birth model. This model integrates a constant velocity model with a set of grid-oriented birth processes, offering a practical solution for scenarios where targets are expected to follow specific directions. The proposed PMBM filter with the partially grid-oriented birth model is implemented for sensor administration. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance compared to standard PMBM filters with isotropic birth models, particularly in situations involving limited sensor coverage. Furthermore, the simulations highlight the practical value of the PMBM framework for sensor administration tasks. Simulation results also indicate that the filter's performance improves with increased sensor coverage and a higher number of potential target birth directions. Additionally, the simulations show that the performance degrades as the time interval between sensor scans lengthens. Finally, real data from the Air Force Research Laboratory's sensor administration trial are utilized to validate the simulations. The simulations and real data results collectively confirm that the partially grid-oriented birth model aligns well with the actual motion characteristics of radars in the trial. Consequently, the simulations and real data analysis suggest that the PMBM filter with the partially grid-oriented birth model is a viable solution for sensor administration. Future work will explore the application of this filter in broader sensor management scenarios. The source code for the simulations is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/PMBM-PO-Direction.

Soccer represents a dynamic, non-deterministic environment where strategic decisions are influenced by the current match state, the specific phase of play, and the time remaining. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved significant success in games like Go and Atari, its application to soccer remains limited. This study introduces a novel state representation and a hierarchical actor-critic algorithm tailored for soccer. When evaluated against a standard baseline and a policy gradient approach using real-world data from the 2018/2019 Serie A season, our method demonstrated superior performance in terms of expected goals (xG) and actual goals scored. Furthermore, the agent learned context-aware policies that align with human intuition, offering actionable insights for coaches and players during critical match moments. The source code and dataset are accessible at: https://github.com/AbderrahimBoussaid/Enhanced_Soccer_Policies.

This study introduces a novel technique for acquiring two-dimensional laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) data across an extensive area using a single-point LDV sensor through distant control. The approach involves directing the LDV's laser beam onto the target via a mirror system, enabling the sensor to gather 2D measurements by altering the beam's angle of incidence. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated using a single-point LDV system equipped with a linear polarizing beamsplitter and a rotating mirror to control the laser's direction. Results indicate that the LDV's sensitivity can be adjusted by varying the angle of incidence, and the system can capture 2D data over a large surface. Furthermore, the collected data aligns well with data obtained from a commercial 2D LDV system. These findings suggest that this technique offers a cost-effective solution for measuring large areas with high spatial resolution, making it valuable for applications such as structural health monitoring. The proposed method is detailed step-by-step, and the resulting 2D data can be acquired using either a single or multiple LDV systems. Finally, a comparison is made between data collected via the proposed technique and that from a commercial 2D LDV system. This study examines the linear and nonlinear spectral characteristics, along with orbital stability, of ground state solutions for the one-dimensional Klein--Gordon equation coupled with an anharmonic oscillator potential. The analysis begins with a detailed investigation of the operator defining the equation's spectrum. Subsequently, the spectral and orbital stability of ground states are thoroughly examined. The findings indicate that nonlinear spectral instability is a universal feature for anharmonic potentials where the mass at infinity is lower than the initial mass. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that spectral instability at the positive eigenvalue $\mu_1$ corresponds directly to linear and nonlinear orbital instability of the ground state. Finally, the research explores the existence of excited states and their associated spectral and orbital stability properties. These results are significant for understanding the long-term dynamical behavior of solutions. Identifying semantic change (ISC) in natural language remains a significant challenge, particularly because existing methods often fail to leverage recent advances in contextualized language representations. This study evaluates two contextualized frameworks—BERT and RoBERTa—for detecting potential instances of ISC. We introduce a novel dataset comprising 1,000 verified examples of lexical semantic change drawn from Wiktionary's discussion pages. Furthermore, we curate a second dataset of 10,000 candidate ISC pairs from Wiktionary lemmatized titles for potential identification. Our findings indicate that contextualized frameworks can effectively identify known instances of lexical semantic change within lexicon resources, provided they are supported by carefully constructed positive examples. Additionally, we observe that both frameworks can uncover previously unrecognized potential ISC cases in words with extensive usage, which may serve as valuable starting points for manual verification. To facilitate future research, we release both datasets and our associated tools at https://github.com/linguistiq/Contextualized-ISC. Ultimately, we conclude that contextualized frameworks hold promise for identifying potential lexical semantic change, yet they should be viewed as a preliminary step requiring further investigation. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for creating lexicon resources and dictionaries.

We investigate the spin distribution of 100 active massive black holes to refine constraints on ultralight scalar and vector particles, which would manifest as ultra-light bosons (UB) through superradiance. This mechanism halts black hole spin-up when the angular frequency aligns with a specific UB mass range. Our analysis indicates that the spin distribution of this sample exhibits a cutoff near a dimensionless value of 0.9, supporting the existence of such ultra-light bosons. Consequently, we derive a new, tighter upper limit for the UB mass of $m_{\rm UB} < 1.0 \times 10^{-11} (\frac{M_{\rm BH}}{10^9 M_{\odot}}) h^{-1}$ GeV. Given that this constraint relies on the cutoff in the spin distribution, it is most effective for black holes with high spins. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin distribution of the Milky Way's central black hole, Sgr A*, is consistent with this proposed cutoff. Finally, we establish a lower bound for the UB mass of $m_{\rm UB} > 10^{-19}$ GeV, applicable to both ultralight scalar and vector particles. These findings suggest that future gravitational wave detectors could potentially detect oscillations in ultra-light bosonic fields. Such detection would provide evidence for new physics beyond the standard model, potentially offering a solution to the dark matter problem. This study employs a Monte Carlo method to simulate the path integral formulation of a driven quantum harmonic oscillator. The simulation utilizes a Metropolis algorithm, which accepts or rejects moves based on the system's action. We examine how the action influences the acceptance rate and its impact on Monte Carlo sampling efficiency. Furthermore, we compare the Monte Carlo results with exact analytical solutions. The simulation was implemented in C++ and executed on a Windows 10 system with an Intel Core i7-8700K processor. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Path-Integral-Technique-to-Driven-Quantum-Harmonic-Oscillator-using-Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo-Approaches. Our findings indicate that the acceptance rate is directly proportional to the amplitude of the driving force. Additionally, the Monte Carlo results align closely with the exact solutions, confirming the validity of this Monte Carlo approach for simulating quantum harmonic oscillators. This method can be extended to simulate other quantum systems.

We introduce a calculus for reasoning about the probabilistic behaviors of quantum programs, extending the quantum relational Hoare calculus with expectations. This system integrates a predicate-style precondition and postcondition with a quantitative expectation operator. We define a sound operational semantics and prove the calculus's soundness regarding this semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the calculus's utility by deriving sound rules for verifying quantum programs against an anticipated formal method. The calculus is implemented via a Modula-2 to Idris compiler, which supports the automation of proof steps. Additionally, we present an automated tactic for reasoning about program correctness using expectations. Finally, we validate the calculus through multiple examples, including the verification of a probabilistic lifting lemma and the correctness of a quantum program designed to test the Bell inequality.

This study addresses the bias inherent in the inferred line-of-sight (LOS) vector magnetic field ($B_{\rm los}$) from solar vector magnetic field (VMF) data, a distortion caused by the inversion process. We demonstrate that this bias is indistinguishable from actual variations in $B_{\rm los}$ and can be misinterpreted as a rotation of the magnetic field direction. To counteract this, we introduce a novel method for correcting the inferred $B_{\rm los}$, which simultaneously yields a new estimation of the uncertainty in the LOS component. Furthermore, we propose a technique to correct the azimuthal angle ($\phi$) directly, rendering it independent of the inversion-derived $B_{\rm los}$. Utilizing high-resolution spectral data from the solar photosphere, we applied these corrections to both synthetic and observational data. Our results indicate that the corrected $\phi$ aligns more closely with the true value than the uncorrected version, and the inferred $B_{\rm los}$ exhibits reduced scatter when compared to the actual values. These findings suggest that correcting bias in the inferred $B_{\rm los}$ and $\phi$ can enhance the accuracy of the vertical and azimuthal components of the vector magnetic field, respectively. Consequently, these corrections are vital for improving the reliability of magnetic field data used in solar physics research and for developing data-driven models in solar physics and space weather forecasting. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/AnirbanMukherjee/BiasCorrection.

This paper examines the boolean structure of $W(\Gamma)$, defined as the collection of involutions within a right-angled Coxeter group $W(\Gamma)$ associated with a graph $\Gamma$. We demonstrate that $W(\Gamma)$ forms a boolean algebra if and only if the graph $\Gamma$ is a complete multipartite graph. Furthermore, we analyze the boolean structure of $W(\Gamma)$ when $\Gamma$ is a tree, providing a characterization of the corresponding covering poset. As an application, we derive a lower bound for the size of the boolean algebra generated by the involution of an affine Weyl group.

This paper investigates timelike Bertrand curves within the class of timelike manifolds that admit a specific connection, termed the modified semi-Riemannian connection. It is demonstrated that, under this modified connection, the definition of a timelike Bertrand curve aligns with that of a timelike curve possessing two linearly independent curvatures. Furthermore, it is proven that a timelike curve qualifies as a modified geodesic if and only if its two curvatures satisfy a particular condition. Finally, the concept of a modified harmonic curve is introduced, and it is shown that a timelike Bertrand curve is a modified harmonic curve precisely when its two curvatures fulfill a specific relationship.

This study evaluates the impact of loss function modifications on the performance of deep learning models for image classification. The analysis covers three standard loss functions—cross entropy, focal, and generalized focal—across three architectures: a convolutional neural network, a vision transformer, and a hybrid model. Results indicate that altering the loss function yields minimal performance gains, with the focal loss variant delivering the most significant improvement. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that increasing the gamma parameter in the generalized focal loss does not necessarily enhance performance; instead, it can lead to performance degradation. Consequently, the findings suggest that shifting focus toward optimizing other model components, such as network architecture, hyperparameters, and data preparation, would be more effective for improving classification outcomes. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/LossFunction.

We introduce ATOMIC, an atlas of machine common knowledge enabling the inference of if-then reasoning across a broad spectrum of commonsense reasoning tasks. This system encompasses multiple reasoning types, including natural language inference (NLI), commonsense entailment (CE), adversarial entailment (AdvsEnt), and adversarial contradiction (AdvsCon), as well as various NLI reasoning styles such as textual, factual, abstract, and unsupported. By leveraging a collection of if-then reasoning pairs, ATOMIC facilitates the training of models capable of inferring such pairs from both natural language sentences and image captions. To achieve this, we developed a suite of if-then reasoning inference models covering a wide range of commonsense reasoning models and if-then reasoning types. These models were trained on existing datasets of natural language reasoning pairs. Furthermore, we constructed a comprehensive dataset of if-then reasoning pairs in natural language, which serves as the foundation for developing an atlas of image-based natural language reasoning pairs. Finally, we created an interactive website that allows users to query these image-based pairs through both image inputs and natural language inputs. Our dataset and atlas are accessible at http://atomic commons. ai/. The source code for our if-then reasoning inference models and the generation of image-based pairs can be found at https://github. com/ATOMIC-Commonsense/ATOMIC-Source-Code. The interactive atlas website is available at http://atomic. common sense. ai/.

Video forecasting represents a significant yet challenging task in computer vision, with potential applications ranging from autonomous driving to public safety. Existing methods typically rely on a single global representation to predict future frames, which often fails to capture the complex characteristics of video data. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages a dual representation to more effectively model video complexity. The method begins by decomposing input videos into foreground and background components, which are processed separately through two distinct networks to generate predictions. These predictions are then combined to produce the final output. Extensive experiments conducted on three standard datasets—UCF101, UEA, and HMDB51—demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits strong generalization capabilities, outperforming other models on unseen datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/Innovative-View-Video-Forecasting-Utilizing-a-Dual-Representation.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted by $\beta(G)$, represents the smallest size of a resolving set for $G$. Similarly, the dimension under the shortened metric, written as $\beta_s(G)$, is defined as the minimum cardinality of a set $R$ that resolves $G$ when distances are measured via the shortened metric $d_s$. It is established that $\beta_s(G) \leq \beta(G)$. This study examines the relationship between $\beta_s(G)$ and $\beta(G)$ across various graph families, offering both theoretical insights and computational findings. Additionally, we characterize trees and graphs with specific structural properties for which $\beta_s(G) = \beta(G) - 1$. Our results indicate that for any graph $G$, the inequality $\beta_s(G) \geq \beta(G) - 1$ holds true. We also determine the exact values of $\beta_s(G)$ for graphs with diameter 3 and 4, and for complete multipartite graphs. Finally, we identify the graphs $G$ that maximize $\beta_s(G)$ given a fixed number of vertices and edges.

Heart sounds serve as a vital indicator for diagnosing cardiovascular disorders, yet their analysis is complicated by the presence of background noise, which degrades the performance of automatic classification systems. This study introduces a novel framework for heart sound categorization that explicitly addresses additive noise through a two-stage approach. Initially, a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) with a residual structure is trained to predict and remove background noise from heart sound signals. Subsequently, a second DCNN classifier processes the cleaned signals to determine the heart sound category. To further enhance classification accuracy, we incorporate a deformation module into the final layer of the classifier. This module employs a fully convolutional architecture to learn optimal deformations for the extracted acoustic features, thereby improving category recognition. Experimental results demonstrate that our end-to-end framework significantly outperforms traditional methods, achieving an F1 score of 0.89 on the noisy PhysioNet/CinC 2017 dataset. Additionally, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, surpassing other approaches on the cleaner PhysioNet/CinC 2013 dataset. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/HeartSoundCategorization.

We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions, the velocity process associated with a specific family of interfaces converges to a diffusion process governed by a skew Brownian motion with drift. This convergence holds true for both conservative and non-conservative dynamics. Furthermore, we establish that the velocity process fully characterizes the law of the interface, a result that extends to non-conservative dynamics as well. Finally, we show that the law of the ASEP with simple asymptotic initial conditions can be derived from the law of the corresponding stepped initial condition. As a direct application, we utilize these findings to determine the distribution of the height at the origin for ASEP governed by simple asymptotic initial conditions.

The rapid spread of SARS-CoV-2 has driven the development of numerous mathematical models to forecast epidemic trajectories, evaluate intervention strategies, and estimate epidemiological parameters. While these models have been valuable for specific tasks, there is no single framework capable of addressing all objectives. This paper offers a concise review of existing models, organized by their underlying mathematical structures. We highlight the strengths and limitations of each approach and propose a unified framework that integrates the most effective elements of current models to meet diverse goals. Furthermore, we discuss the necessary epidemiological assumptions and data requirements for implementing this comprehensive framework. Finally, we examine how mathematical models can be effectively utilized to tackle various challenges arising during an epidemic.

We examine the connection between Baryon Mass ($M_{\rm bar}$) and Star Formation Rate (SFR) for central galaxies in the mass range $10^{9.5}-10^{11.2} M_{\rm \odot}$ across redshifts $0.00<z<2.0$, utilizing BAYEULCHEA and total Baryon Mass estimates derived from NFDeep1.1 photometric data. Our analysis indicates that this relationship is influenced by Specific Baryon Mass ($\mu_{\rm bar}$) and Baryon Fraction ($f_{\rm bar}$), which are themselves affected by Halo Mass ($M_{\rm h}$) and Concentration ($c$). Furthermore, the slope of the $M_{\rm bar}$-SFR relation varies with $\mu_{\rm bar}$ and $f_{\rm bar}$; specifically, the turnover observed at high Baryon Masses is driven by a flattening of the $M_{\rm h}$-SFR relation. We find that bulge fraction ($f_{\rm b}$) and bulge-to-total ratio ($B/T$) are strongly correlated with both $M_{\rm bar}$ and $\mu_{\rm bar}$. Additionally, $f_{\rm b}$ and $B/T$ exhibit significant positive correlations with $M_{\rm h}$, $c$, $\mu_{\rm bar}$, and $f_{\rm bar}$, while showing negative correlations with SFR and the specific SFR ($sSFR$). These results suggest that the turnover in the $M_{\rm bar}$-SFR relation at high masses is motivated by an increase in $f_{\rm b}$ and $B/T$, which in turn are driven by rising $M_{\rm h}$, $c$, $\mu_{\rm bar}$, and $f_{\rm bar}$. Consequently, the $M_{\rm h}$-sSFR and $c$-sSFR relations are shaped by the suppression of star formation within bulges. Finally, the $M_{\rm bar}$-SFR relation appears to be more sensitive to $f_{\rm b}$ and $B/T$ than the $M_{\rm h}$-SFR relation is.

This work introduces a cross-lingual sentiment analysis system for Romanian, a low-resource language, utilizing a multi-task learning approach. The model was trained on two datasets: Romanian and English. It was evaluated on the Romanian dataset using both the original dataset and a held-out portion. Results indicate that the system's performance on Romanian sentiment prediction is comparable to that on English. Furthermore, the model's performance on the Romanian dataset improved when evaluated against the held-out data. These findings suggest that incorporating the language prediction task as an auxiliary objective during training enhances sentiment prediction accuracy for Romanian. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AndreeaMihai/CrossLinguisticSentiment. The authors acknowledge funding from the Romanian Executive Agency for Higher Education, Research, Development, and Innovation (UEFISCDI) under project PN-III-P4-ID-PCE-2020-2231.

We address the title question by demonstrating that the outer disk of HL-1, a low-mass X-ray binary with a 2.9-hour orbital period, is spinning up via the ingestion of an inner planet. This finding provides evidence for the existence of such planets around low-mass X-ray binaries. Our analysis indicates that HL-1's neutron star is accreting from a low-density, outer, gas-rich disk, which exhibits a complex structure characterized by a central hole, an inner annulus, and an outer ring. The central hole is likely responsible for the X-ray variability observed in HL-1. Furthermore, the outer ring may be responsible for the detected radio emission. We conclude by proposing a model for the complex structure of HL-1's disk and discussing the implications of our results for the formation of low-mass X-ray binaries. The source data for this study is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10632101.

Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, posing significant challenges for human detection. While deep learning models have been effective at identifying false news from verified sources, they require extensive labeled datasets. Such data is scarce for verified multimodal news, which includes both text and images. To address this limitation, we introduce MetaFNet, a novel end-to-end framework for detecting verified multimodal fake news using meta-learning and neural process networks. This approach enables the identification of fake news from verified sources without relying on specific labels for individual articles. Furthermore, MetaFNet can generalize to detect fake news from unverified sources. Our experiments demonstrate that MetaFNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in identifying both verified and unverified multimodal fake news. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/MetaFNet.

Golay complementary sequences (GCS) have been extensively studied due to their ideal autocorrelation properties, which are valuable in radar, sonar, and wireless communications. Recently, GCS pairs have been applied to construct Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and Golay complementary sets (GCSets). While numerous constructions of GCSets exist, they are typically derived from GCA pairs, which are limited by the constraints inherent in GCA pairs. This paper introduces three novel constructions of GCSets utilizing the product of DFT matrices and the Kronecker product of GCS pairs and Golay complementary sets (GCSets) of vectors. These constructions yield GCSets with larger sizes than previously reported. Specifically, for a prime $p$ and integer $n$, a GCSet with size $N = p^{2n}$ can be achieved when $p \le 3$, and $N = 5^{2n}$ is possible for $n \le 2$. Furthermore, a GCSet with size $N = 7^{2n}$ is feasible for $n \le 1$. To the best of our knowledge, these represent the largest GCSets constructed to date. Finally, a connection between GCSets and Golay orthogonal sets (GOSets) of vectors is established, and a new construction of GOSets is proposed. The validity of these constructions is confirmed through numerical examples. Potential applications of GCSets in sequences and arrays are also discussed. The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
  (i) Three new constructions of GCSets are developed, achieving sizes larger than existing methods.
  (ii) A relationship between GCSets and GOSets is identified, leading to a novel construction of GOSets.
  (iii) The constructions of GCSets and GOSets are verified using numerical examples.
  (iv) Potential applications of GCSets in both GCSets and GCS pairs are explored.
  The detailed constructions are outlined in Sections II through IV, with Section V discussing potential applications of GCSets. Concluding remarks are provided in Section VI. Lesion synthesis represents a significant advancement in medical imaging, offering a practical solution to the scarcity of annotated lesion data required for training deep learning models. While recent methods have primarily focused on specific lesion types like pneumonias or retinal abnormalities, there has been limited progress in developing a generalizable framework for creating synthetic images across diverse lesion categories. This study introduces a novel generalizable approach to generate various cerebral lesions using a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE). The model operates in two phases: initially, a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) is trained on healthy brain images to learn their underlying distribution; subsequently, a second adversarial network is introduced to transform these healthy images into ones containing lesions. Experimental results demonstrate that the PAVAE successfully produces synthetic cerebral lesions, and when combined with existing datasets, it effectively enhances the performance of lesion classification models. Furthermore, the synthesized images exhibit high fidelity, as confirmed by both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments. The trained models and generated datasets are accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/PAVAE-for-Cerebral-Lesions. Ultimately, this generalizable framework holds promise for expanding medical imaging datasets and accelerating research into the detection and classification of diverse cerebral lesions. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/PAVAE-for-Cerebral-Lesions.

Feature extraction serves as a critical preprocessing step for comparative learning tasks, including ranking, listwise learning, and learning to rank. Although numerous methods have been proposed, they often lack unified theoretical foundations and rely on ad hoc designs. This paper introduces a unified framework for feature extraction grounded in comparative learning. Initially, we define a comparative feature space and a corresponding embedding function. Subsequently, we introduce a novel embedding method that leverages both comparative and absolute features. We demonstrate that this approach yields a unified framework for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction. Empirical results show that our framework outperforms existing unsupervised and supervised methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework enables the development of a unified model capable of handling both comparative and non-comparative learning tasks. Experiments confirm that this model surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches for both learning types. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYong01/Unified-Feature-Extraction.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized to automate tasks across various domains, yet their capabilities are constrained by the sheer volume of domain-specific knowledge required. Integrating structured knowledge, such as knowledge graphs, with LLMs offers a promising solution to these limitations. This paper introduces ABILITY, a framework that enables prompt-based LLMs to acquire additional knowledge for automated task completion. We evaluated ABILITY against state-of-the-art methods using three distinct knowledge graphs and three downstream datasets. The results demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving a 10.5% increase in accuracy on the TREC dataset, a 12.1% gain on WikiHop, and a 13.3% improvement on TriviaQA. Furthermore, we release the source code and a curated dataset to support future research in this area. The framework is accessible at https://github.com/roberta12/ABILITY.

Non-linear interactions between electromagnetic fields and vacuum energy are significant in high-energy physics. In this study, we investigate the non-linear charged AdS black hole solution derived from the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) action. By analyzing the thermodynamic phase transitions of this black hole through its shadow radius, we establish a correspondence between the shadow radius and temperature. Our results indicate that the shadow radius initially decreases and then increases as temperature rises, exhibiting a V-shaped curve. Furthermore, we identify a critical point where a second-order phase transition occurs. Finally, we explore the relationship between the shadow radius and other thermodynamic variables, including entropy, heat capacity, and Yang-Mills charge. These findings suggest that the shadow radius can serve as an effective probe for examining the thermodynamic properties of black holes. The connection between the shadow radius and various thermodynamic variables is illustrated via phase portraits and graphs. Additionally, we demonstrate that the shadow radius is independent of the observer's position. Our analysis of the EPYM black hole's shadow radius reveals that non-linear effects cause the shadow radius to shrink, implying that the non-linearity of the Yang-Mills field influences the black hole's size. This work offers a novel perspective on the thermodynamics of non-linear charged AdS black holes by utilizing the shadow radius. The results may assist in detecting phase transitions in black holes through their shadows and provide insights into the non-linear characteristics of the Yang-Mills field. Future research could explore the influence of Yang-Mills non-linearity on the gravitational wave signatures of black hole mergions. The methodology presented here is applicable to other black hole models, potentially aiding in the detection of novel black hole phases. This study introduces a measure of entanglement based on the Wigner-Weyl quasi-probability distribution for continuous-variable systems, utilizing the entanglement of formation. We demonstrate that for Gaussian states, this metric aligns with entanglement witnesses derived from covariance matrices, which are inherently positive. Leveraging the Wootters formula, we formulate an entanglement metric within the optical entanglement tomogram framework. We also define an entanglement metric for optical entanglement tomograms for non-Gaussian states and derive an entanglement metric for non-separable Schrödinger cat states within the same framework. Additionally, we propose an entanglement metric for non-Gaussian squeezed vacuum states in this framework. As a novel contribution, we introduce an metric to quantify the onset of synchronization in non-Gaussian squeezed vacuum states. To validate these metrics, we calculate entanglement and synchronization onset metrics for specific non-Gaussian optical entanglement and synchronization tomograms. The results indicate that the entanglement metric in the optical entanglement tomogram framework for continuous-variable systems is effective for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, while the metric for the beginning of synchronization in the optical entanglement tomogram framework applies specifically to non-Gaussian states. Furthermore, we establish that in the optical entanglement tomogram framework, the metric for entanglement of formation and metrics for both entanglement and its beginning in Gaussian and non-Gaussian continuous-variable systems are equivalent to metrics derived from the optical entanglement Wigner function framework. Finally, we present an metric for the degree of non-locality in optical entanglement and synchronization tomograms. The branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ is measured to be $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L)=\left(1.80^{+0.24}_{-0.21}\left(\mathrm{stat}\right)^{+0.13}_{-0.11}\left(\mathrm{syst}\right)\right)\times10^{-3}$, contingent upon adopting the branching fraction $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\pi^0)=0.53\%$ from Particle Data Group averages. The branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ is determined as $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L)=\left(1.52^{+0.24}_{-0.21}\left(\mathrm{stat}\right)^{+0.13}_{-0.11}\left(\mathrm{syst}\right)\right)\times10^{-3}$. This paper addresses the challenge of constructing the complete diagram of $M(\mu)$, a multiplicity free module over a Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{g}(A_{2,1})$, utilizing only a partial subposet of its lattice. We demonstrate that the lattice of submodules of $M(\mu)$ can be generated from a collection of specific submodules, which are either simple or Borel. Furthermore, we establish that this lattice is distributive. Finally, we provide a comprehensive characterization of all distributive lattices arising from the submodules of $M(\mu)$. These findings are applied to derive the full diagram of $M(\mu)$ from a selected set of submodules. As an additional contribution, we present a complete classification of all distributive lattices associated with the submodules of $M(\mu)$. The resulting diagram of the $A_{2,1}$ multiplicity free module $M(0,0,0)$ is illustrated in Figure 1.1.

This study examines biharmonic hypersurfaces characterized by repetitive Laplacian operators within Euclidean space. We demonstrate that a product of two spheres with distinct radii in Euclidean space is biharmonic if and only if its radions satisfy a specific algebraic condition, and in this scenario, the Laplacian operator repeats twice. Furthermore, we prove that no other biharmonic hypersurfaces exist with repetitive Laplacian operators in Euclidean space. Additionally, we provide a classification of biharmonic hypersurfaces where the Laplacian operator repeats exactly $k$ times. Finally, we establish that for any $n$-dimensional sphere in Euclidean space, the multiplicity of its Laplacian operator as an eigenfunction of the Bernstein operator is at most $n+1$. These findings generalize and extend the results reported in reference [10].

A subset $A$ of the non-negative integers is termed $p/q$-recognizable if the formal power series associated with $A$ is rational and possesses poles exclusively at points of the form $\zeta (\sqrt[q]{p})^k$, where $\zeta$ is a root of unity. This concept was initially explored by Berstel, Perrin, and Reutenauer under the name $p/q$-regular. The set of non-negative integers satisfying this property is referred to as a $p/q$-identifiable set. While it is established that every finite set is $p/q$-identifiable, it was recently demonstrated by Krob and the current authors that no infinite arithmetic progression shares this characteristic. In this work, we introduce the notion of a $p/q$-recognizable language and prove that a language is $p/q$-recognizable if and only if it is regular and its characteristic sequence forms an ultimately periodic sequence that constitutes a $p/q$-identifiable set. Furthermore, we show that for any prime $p$ and integer $q \ge 2$, the set of primes constitutes a $p/q$-identifiable set. Finally, we provide a characterization of identifiable sets within the family of $k$-regular sequences.

When an adhesive tape is peeled, the sound generated exhibits intermittent bursts, a phenomenon known as acoustic emission (AE). These bursts are influenced by pulling speed, tape dimensions, and material properties. This study examines the acoustic spectrum of an acrylic tape (Permabond 100) pulled from a surface at various speeds. The resulting spectrum displays distinct peaks, indicating hidden periodicity in the burst signals. Furthermore, the positions of these peaks shift with the pulling speed, suggesting that the periodicity of the bursts is intrinsic to the dynamics of the AE bursts themselves. Analysis of the burst signals reveals chaotic characteristics, which can be described using a chaotic model. Additionally, the acoustic spectrum shows a transition from discrete peaks to a continuous band as the pulling speed increases, a behavior analogous to period-doubling routes to chaos observed in chaotic time series. These findings suggest that the stick-slip dynamics responsible for acoustic bursts during tape peeling possess ordered, chaotic characteristics similar to those found in chaotic oscillating systems. The observed acoustic spectrum aligns with the power spectrum of a Duffing oscillator, implying that the stick-slip dynamics of the adhesive tape can be modeled using a concealed order within the chaotic acoustic emission bursts via a chaotic oscillating model. To validate this model, we measured the vibration of the tape at the slip point using a laser vibrometer, confirming that the vibration frequency matches the peaks identified in the acoustic spectrum. We also analyzed the force required to peel the tape, demonstrating that both the acoustic spectrum and the vibration frequency are directly linked to the pulling speed and the peeling force. These results indicate that the chaotic acoustic bursts during peeling arise from ordered stick-slip dynamics governed by the applied pulling force. Consequently, the acoustic spectrum and burst periodicity can serve as indicators for determining the peeling force and predicting the burst periodicity for a given force. This research offers new insights into the stick-slip dynamics of an adhesive tape during peeling, suggesting that the chaotic acoustic bursts conceal an ordered structure determined by the peeling force. Such an ordered structure within chaotic acoustic bursts may also exist in other systems exhibiting acoustic bursts during frictional sliding.

Point clouds, which consist of unordered sets of 3D coordinates, are a prevalent data type in domains like robotics, computer vision, and autonomous driving. Their inherent set-like structure creates challenges for deep learning models, which typically assume fixed input structures. To address this, recent methods like Set Abstracting Networks (SAN) and Set of Sets Transformers (ToSoT) introduce extra layers of structure to facilitate learning. However, these added structural elements can hinder learning by introducing redundancy and noise. This paper proposes Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), a lightweight technique designed to reduce noise in point cloud structures. We demonstrate that TPC can be integrated into various neural network architectures, including SAN, ToSoT, and PointNet, without requiring architectural changes. Extensive experiments show that incorporating TPC into SAN, ToSoT, and PointNet significantly boosts performance across multiple tasks, such as classification, semantic segmentation, and detection. Furthermore, these performance gains are achieved with fewer parameters and faster training and inference times compared to baseline models. The source code is available at https://github.com/tpc-smoothing/TPC.

This paper introduces a geometric framework for evaluating the correctness of program transformations, which encompasses both semantic equivalence and optimization validity. The framework offers a unified, constructive approach to correctness evaluation that relies on a constructive semantic model. It enables the automatic derivation of correctness proofs for a wide range of transformations, including variable renaming, dead code elimination, constant folding, inlining, and various interprocedural optimizations. Furthermore, the framework supports the derivation of correctness proofs for combinations of transformations and can be integrated with existing equivalence checkers to validate transformations for which a constructive proof is unfeasible. We implemented this framework within the Irocks interprocedural semantic analyzer and demonstrated its utility through the derivation of correctness proofs for numerous transformations in the CompCert C compiler. The source code and detailed walkthroughs of these derivations are accessible at https://github.com/irocks-framework/irocks-demo-compcert.

This paper offers a concise proof of the existence of $\ell$-adic Serre weights for $\mathrm{GL}_2$ corresponding to irreducible diagonalizable characteristic zero representations of the local Galois group, utilizing Kummer theory. Additionally, we establish that these weights are unique when the associated character is generic. Our approach relies on constructing explicit Euler systems for nearly ordinary $p$-adic automorphic forms on $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\ell)$, which are twisted by local characters at primes dividing $N$. These Euler systems are then compared against explicit Euler-Poincaré formulas for the cohomology of Shimura varieties of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}) \times \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\ell)$. It is important to note that our construction of these Euler systems does not require the weight to be a "classical" Serre weight. Furthermore, this work serves as a companion to the second author's study on the $p$-adic Langlands correspondence for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})$ and the compact quotient $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$. The existence and uniqueness of the weights under consideration are crucial for defining the relevant eigencurve. Finally, we demonstrate that our constructed Euler systems remain valid even when the associated weight lacks a classical Serre weight, thereby enabling the definition of an eigencurve in such cases. This extension is significant for the second author's research, as it allows for a broader formulation of the eigencurve. Ultimately, we prove that the eigencurve associated with the tuple $(K=1,N,\ell=2,a=\overline{\chi})$ exists and is smooth in a neighborhood of a specific set of classical points.

This study introduces a novel approach to precisely detecting damage initiation in self-sensing composite materials via electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While EIT offers a non-destructive, full-field method for monitoring damage, it has historically struggled with exact localization due to the ill-posed nature of the inverse problem. To overcome this, we combine a global optimization genetic algorithm with a local optimization Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Quesnel (BFGQ) algorithm to achieve exact localization. The effectiveness of this hybrid strategy is validated through numerical simulations and experiments on a carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminate. Results demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately identify both the onset and location of damage, providing a complete characterization of the damage event. Furthermore, the study examines how sensor distribution and the number of damage sites influence localization accuracy. Ultimately, this work presents a complete characterization of damage initiation in CFRP laminates using electrical impedance tomography, which is particularly valuable for detecting delamination in self-sensing composites. The proposed technique holds significant potential for enhancing the safety of aerospace structures and other high-risk engineering applications.
